What is the atomic number of Oxygen?
Oxygen is a chemical element; it has the symbol O and its atomic number is 8.
In what year was Werner Heisenberg born?
Werner Heisenberg: Heisenberg published his Umdeutung paper in 1925, a major reinterpretation of old quantum theory.
In what year was Glutathione discovered?
Glutathione (GSH,) is a tripeptide made of the amino acids glutamate, cysteine, and glycine.
In what year was Morphine discovered?
Morphine, formerly known as morphium, is an opiate found naturally in opium, a dark brown resin produced by drying the latex of opium poppies (Papaver somniferum).

Which country is Sukhoi Su-35 from?
Sukhoi Su-35: Soviet Union. The type was originally developed by the Soviet Union from the Su-27 and was known as the Su-27M.
Who is credited with discovering Palladium?
Palladium: William Hyde Wollaston. Palladium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Pd and atomic number 46.
Who is credited with discovering Pectin?

Who is credited with discovering Oxygen?

The simplest alkyne, this colorless gas owes its straight-line shape to a carbon-carbon triple bond — and though pure it's odorless, commercial grades reek thanks to impurities. What is it?
Acetylene (systematic name: ethyne) is a chemical compound with the formula C2H2 and structure HCCH.
A military pilot who became the first astronaut representing Turkey, he reached the International Space Station on 18 January 2024 aboard the Axiom Mission 3 flight — who is he?
Alper Gezeravcı (born 2 December 1979) is a military pilot and the first Turkish astronaut.
This scientific discipline bridges biology and sociology, studying human behavior, cultures, societies, and languages across time. What field is it?

Anthropology is the scientific study of humanity that crosses biology and sociology, concerned with human behavior, human biology, cultures, societies, and linguistics, in both the present and past, including archaic humans.
This common vision condition occurs when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped rather than spherical, causing blurred vision at any distance. What is it?
Astigmatism is a type of refractive error due to rotational asymmetry in the eye's refractive power.
Strawberries, blackcurrants and blueberries all count in the kitchen sense — though botanists would object, since the culinary meaning of this word differs from the scientific one. What word?
Berry is a small, pulpy, and often edible fruit.
This family of cloven-hoofed, ruminant mammals includes cattle, bison, buffalo, antelopes, sheep, and goats across 143 living species — name the family?
Bovidae is the biological family of cloven-hoofed, ruminant mammals that includes cattle, bison, buffalo, antelopes, and goat-antelopes such as sheep and goats.
Sole living family in the mammalian suborder Tylopoda, which group unites camels with llamas and their South American relatives?
Camelidae is a family of mammals belonging to the ungulate order Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates) and the only living family in the suborder Tylopoda.
This class of ribbon-like parasitic flatworms sheds egg-packed body segments called proglottids into the environment to infect new hosts — what is this class called (scientific name)?
Cestoda is a class of parasitic worms in the flatworm phylum (Platyhelminthes).
This anatomical term for the hollow between a woman's breasts was coined in its modern sense by a Hollywood censor reviewing the 1943 film starring Jane Russell — what is the term?
Cleavage (breasts) is the narrow depression or hollow between the breasts of a woman.
This group of related RNA viruses causes respiratory illnesses ranging from the mild common cold to deadly diseases like SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 — what's this virus family called?
Coronavirus are a group of related RNA viruses that cause diseases in mammals and birds.

Native to Madagascar and grown as an ornamental tree throughout the tropics, this legume species has fern-like leaves and a flamboyant summer display of orange-red flowers; its wild origin wasn't confirmed until 1932. What tree is this?
Delonix regia is a species of flowering plant in the bean family Fabaceae, subfamily Caesalpinioideae native to Madagascar.

Massive enough to be rounded by its own gravity but too small to clear its orbital neighborhood like the solar system's eight major planets, Pluto became the prototype of this category after a 2006 reclassification. Name the category?

Dwarf planet is a small planetary-mass object that is in direct orbit around the Sun, massive enough to be gravitationally rounded, but insufficient to achieve orbital dominance like the eight classical planets of the Solar System.

Often used to keep blood pressure from dropping during anesthesia, this stimulant has also been tried against asthma, obesity, and even narcolepsy — though it's no longer the preferred fix. What is it?
Ephedrine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant and sympathomimetic agent that is often used to prevent low blood pressure during anesthesia.
A Swiss linguist and philosopher who died in 1913, this thinker's ideas shaped 20th-century linguistics, psychoanalysis, and anthropology alike, according to one of his translators — who is he?
Ferdinand de Saussure (26 November 1857 - 22 February 1913) was a Swiss linguist, semiotician and philosopher.

Derived from a Greek word meaning 'milky,' this term names any gravity-bound system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter, ranging from tiny dwarfs to supergiants with a hundred trillion stars. What is it?
Galaxy is a system of stars, stellar remnants, interstellar gas, dust, and dark matter bound together by gravity.
Comprising about 50 species native to tropical regions worldwide, this genus produces roughly 80% of the world's natural fiber and doubles as an oilseed crop — which genus?
Gossypium is a genus of flowering plants in the tribe Gossypieae of the mallow family, Malvaceae, from which cotton is harvested.
In their healthy state these vascular cushions in the anal canal actually help with stool control — it's only when they swell or inflame that they earn the nickname "piles." What are they?
Hemorrhoid (or haemorrhoids), also known as piles, are vascular structures in the anal canal.
Behaviorally and physically dog-like despite being closer kin to felines, this carnivoran's family is the fifth-smallest in its order with only four extant species — what is it?
Hyena (hi-; from Ancient Greek, haina) are feliform carnivoran mammals belonging to the family Hyaenidae (Latin).

Also known by the old names green vitriol and copperas, this heptahydrate salt dissolves in water to form a paramagnetic, octahedral aquo complex and is used medically to fight anemia — which compound is it?
Iron(II) sulfate (British) denotes a range of salts with the formula FeSO4xH2O.

He wrote the first commercial anti-virus software in 1987 and ran twice for the Libertarian presidential nomination — yet later urged people to uninstall the very product that still bears his name. Who is he?
John McAfee (18 September 1945 - 23 June 2021) was a British and American computer programmer, businessman, and two-time U.S.
Striking children as they wean, up to about age five, this protein-deficiency disorder produces edema and a fatty, enlarged liver — what is it called?
Kwashiorkor (-kr) is a form of severe protein malnutrition characterized by edema and an enlarged liver with fatty infiltrates.
Sociable for a big cat and more active by day than its relatives, this savannah hunter is so sexually dimorphic that only the males grow a sweeping mane. Which animal?
Lion (Panthera leo) is a large cat of the genus Panthera, currently ranging only in Sub-Saharan Africa and India.

This German sexologist founded the Scientific-Humanitarian Committee, which carried out what's been called the first advocacy for homosexual and transgender rights — before the Nazis stripped his citizenship in 1933. Who was he?
Magnus Hirschfeld (14 May 1868 - 14 May 1935) was a German physician, sexologist, and LGBTQ advocate whose German citizenship was revoked in 1933 by the Nazi government.
This natural biological transition marks the permanent end of menstrual periods, typically occurring between ages 45 and 55 as estrogen levels decline — what is it?
Menopause is the time when menstrual periods permanently stop, marking the end of the reproductive stage for the female human.

Caused by a poxvirus spread through direct contact, this viral skin infection produces small raised pink lesions with a distinctive dimple in the center, usually clearing on its own within a year — name the condition?
Molluscum contagiosum (MC), sometimes called water warts, is a viral infection of the skin that results in small raised pink lesions with a dimple in the center.
This flexible body part lets the head turn in every direction while its compartments guard the spinal cord and upper airway between head and torso — what is it, also known as the cervix?
Neck is the part of the body in many vertebrates that connects the head to the torso.

Synthesized in 2002 at a lab near Moscow and named in 2016 for the physicist who hunted down the heaviest atoms, this synthetic element claims the highest atomic number and atomic mass of anything yet known — which is it?
Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
Found in organs such as the brain and lungs, inside flatworms, and within leaf cross-sections, this word names an organism's bulk functional tissue — what is it?
Parenchyma is the bulk of functional substance in an animal organ such as the brain or lungs, or a structure such as a tumour.
Made in the body from the amino acid L-phenylalanine, this natural stimulant also turns up in fermented chocolate and inhibits a transporter called VMAT2 — what is it?
Phenethylamine (PEA) is an organic compound, natural monoamine alkaloid, and trace amine, which acts as a central nervous system stimulant in humans.
It looks like a single point of light, but this brightest star of Ursa Minor is actually a triple star system parked near the north celestial pole — what is it?
Polaris is a yellow supergiant star in the northern circumpolar constellation of Ursa Minor.
Found in more than 200 species of mushroom, this inactive compound is a prodrug your body quickly converts to psilocin, a near-cousin of serotonin — what is it?
Psilocybin (4-), is a naturally occurring tryptamine alkaloid and investigational drug found in more than 200 species of mushrooms, with hallucinogenic and serotonergic effects.
This rapidly worsening brain condition can follow a bout of chickenpox or influenza and is strongly associated with aspirin use in children — what syndrome is it?
Reye syndrome is a rapidly worsening brain disease. Signs and symptoms of Reye syndrome may include vomiting, personality changes, confusion, seizures, and loss of consciousness.
A Stanford physicist who also held an English literature degree, in 1983 she became, at 32, the youngest American ever to fly in space. Who is she?
Sally Ride (May 26, 1951-July 23, 2012) was an American astronaut and physicist.

Drawing on tools from anthropology, biology, medicine, psychology, and criminology, this scientific field studies human sexual interests, behaviors, and functions, distinct from purely social commentary on the subject — what is this field called?
Sexology is the scientific study of human sexuality, including human sexual interests, behaviors, and functions.
The largest of the toothed whales and the largest toothed predator alive, this pelagic giant has females who give birth only every four to twenty years — what is it?
Sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) is the largest of the toothed whales and the largest toothed predator.

Which British single-seat fighter plane, the only such aircraft Britain produced continuously throughout World War II, was famous for its innovative elliptical wing designed to be as thin as possible?
Supermarine Spitfire is a British single-seat fighter aircraft that was used by the Royal Air Force and other Allied countries before, during, and after World War II.
Classed among the saurischians and placing them nearer to sauropodomorphs than to ornithischians, these hollow-boned, three-toed dinosaurs were ancestrally meat-eaters — which clade?
Theropoda (from ancient Greek -) is one of the three major clades of dinosaur, alongside Ornithischia and Sauropodomorpha.

Native only to New Zealand and resembling a lizard, this reptile is the sole surviving member of an order that was hugely diverse in the Mesozoic era, with fossils dating to the Middle Triassic — what's the animal?
Tuatara (Mori:; Sphenodon punctatus) is a species of reptile endemic to New Zealand.

This English fashion designer, largely responsible for bringing punk fashion into the mainstream, ran a boutique on King's Road with her partner, whose band helped define the 1970s UK punk scene — who is she?

Vivienne Westwood (ne Swire; 8 April 1941 - 29 December 2022) was an English fashion designer and businesswoman, largely responsible for bringing modern punk and new wave fashions into the mainstream.
The first woman ever to serve as Ukraine's prime minister, this politician held that post in 2005 and again from 2007 to 2010, and now leads the Batkivshchyna political party — who is she?

Yulia Tymoshenko (ne Hrihyan; born 27 November 1960) is a Ukrainian politician, who served as Prime Minister of Ukraine in 2005, and again from 2007 until 2010; the first woman in Ukraine to hold that position.
Nicknamed the 'upside-down tree' for its unusual silhouette, this genus of long-lived African and Malagasy giants was named after a French naturalist — what genus is it?
Adansonia: Genus of trees known as baobab.
Made in the adrenal cortex, this hormone tells the kidney to hang onto sodium and dump potassium, quietly steering your blood pressure and blood volume — what is it?
A colourless gas of nitrogen and hydrogen with a famously pungent smell, this compound has about 70% of its industrial output turned into fertilisers — what is it?
Ammonia: Chemical compound. A stable binary hydride and the simplest pnictogen hydride, ammonia is a colourless gas with a distinctive pungent smell.
Caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis, its skin form starts as a small blister that becomes a painless ulcer with a telltale black center — what infection is this?
Anthrax: Infection caused by Bacillus anthracis bacteria. The skin form presents with a small blister with surrounding swelling that often turns into a painless ulcer with a black center.
Literally meaning "hardening of the arteries," this umbrella term covers vascular disorders marked by abnormal thickening and loss of elasticity in artery walls — what is it called?
Arteriosclerosis: Thickening, hardening and loss of elasticity of the walls of arteries.
Sharing the 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Tomas Lindahl and Paul Modrich, this Turkish-American scientist was honored for mechanistic studies of DNA repair — who is he?
Aziz Sancar: Turkish biochemist and molecular biologist (born 1946)
Built atop an Ilyushin transport and nicknamed 'Mainstay,' this Soviet radar plane had its existence leaked to the West by a spy in 1978 — which aircraft is it?
Beriev A-50: Soviet airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft.
Originally launched as the McDonnell Douglas MD-95, this narrow-body airliner seats up to 134 passengers with twin engines mounted at the tail — which jet?

He won a share of the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics for an effect he discovered as a Cambridge PhD student in 1962 — then, in the 1970s, took up Transcendental Meditation and pursued ideas beyond mainstream science. Who is he?
Named for the Latin word for the first day of the month, this daisy-family genus is commonly called marigold and is prized in herbal and cosmetic products — which plant?
Calendula: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
Its Greek-derived genus name Xylocopa literally means 'wood-cutter,' fitting for an insect that burrows nesting tunnels into dead wood or bamboo — which insect is it?
Carpenter bee: Common name for a genus of bees.

Serving as royal executioner under Louis XVI and later chief executioner of the First Republic, this Frenchman carried out nearly 3,000 executions during his 40-year career, including those of the king, queen, and Robespierre — who is he?

Also bearing the names Krebs and TCA, this loop of biochemical reactions unlocks the energy in nutrients via the oxidation of acetyl-CoA — and is thought to be one of the earliest metabolic components. What is it?
Citric acid cycle: Interconnected biochemical reactions releasing energy.

A member of the true thrushes, this Eurasian songbird whose nominate male is all black breeds across Europe, western Asia, and North Africa and has been introduced to Australia and New Zealand — which bird is it?
Common blackbird: Thrush native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa.
Domesticated in Africa and thriving in sandy, low-rainfall soil, this ancient legume is now grown mostly in Nigeria and Niger, which together supply two-thirds of the world's crop — which plant?
Cowpea: Species of plant. The cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna.
Son of a bass-baritone and born into a family of engineers, this American built his first car at 19, won four F1 Grands Prix, and took Le Mans in 1967 — who was he?
Dan Gurney: American racing driver, engineer and motorsport executive (1931–2018)
Nicknamed 'dumb cane' because its poisonous sap can temporarily rob you of speech, this shade-tolerant tropical houseplant is native to the New World — which genus?
Dieffenbachia: Genus of plants. Dieffenbachia, commonly known as dumb cane or leopard lily, is a genus of tropical flowering plants in the family Araceae.
This plant genus in the mallow family produces the world's most famously pungent fruit, alongside eight other edible-fruit-bearing species — which genus?
Durio: Genus of plants. Several species produce an edible fruit known as durian, the most common species being Durio zibethinus, with eight others producing edible fruit.

The heaviest aircraft ever built by its Brazilian manufacturer, this twin-engine jet transport was developed as a derivative of a regional jetliner, similar in role to the C-130 Hercules. Which aircraft?
Embraer C-390 Millennium: Brazilian military transport aircraft/tanker.
The simplest alkene and the most-produced organic compound on Earth, this colorless gas is also a natural plant hormone used to ripen fruit — what is it?
This principle describes how a changing magnetic field generates an electric current, underpinning the operation of transformers, generators, and motors — what is it called?
Faraday's law of induction: Basic law of electromagnetism.
Patented in 1962 and sold under a brand name synonymous with 'roofies,' this benzodiazepine is notoriously linked to date-rape drug use — what is it?
Flunitrazepam: Benzodiazepine sedative. Flunitrazepam, sold under the brand name Rohypnol among others, is a benzodiazepine used to treat severe insomnia and assist with anesthesia.
Born in ancient Pergamon to a wealthy architect, this Roman-era Greek physician's writings shaped anatomy, physiology, and pharmacology for centuries — who was he?
Galen: Greek physician, surgeon, and philosopher (c. 129–216 AD)
Despite centuries of use in Korean and Chinese traditional medicine, no clinical evidence supports health claims for this Panax-genus root, often sold as a dietary supplement — what is it?
Ginseng: Root of a plant used in herbal preparations.
This junctional area between the torso and thigh, where the lower abdominal wall meets the leg, is commonly strained in a familiar sports injury — what is it called?
Groin: Area between the torso and the thigh. In human anatomy, the groin, also known as the inguinal region or iliac region, is the junctional area between the torso and the thigh.
This wingless insect spends its entire life on the human scalp, sipping blood, and can neither fly nor jump — its short stumpy legs can't even walk well on a flat surface. What tiny freeloader is it?
Head louse: Insect parasite of humans.
This academic discipline studies the methods, sources, and interpretive approaches historians use when writing about the past — what's it called?
Historiography: Study of the methods used by historians.
Defined as a blood level above 5.5 mmol/L, this elevated-potassium condition can trigger a dangerous heart rhythm and even cardiac arrest — what is it called?
Hyperkalemia: Excess potassium in the blood. Normal potassium levels are between 3.5 and 5.0 mmol/L (3.5 and 5.0 mEq/L) with levels above 5.5 mmol/L defined as hyperkalemia.

ISO 56000:2020 defines it as "a new or changed entity, realizing or redistributing value" — but the everyday version is the practical implementation of ideas, the cousin of invention focused on newness, improvement, and the spread of technologies. What's the word?
Innovation: Practical implementation of improvements. Innovation is the practical implementation of ideas that result in the creation or improvements of goods or services.
Mentored by Louis Leakey, this English primatologist spent six decades at Gombe and revealed that chimpanzees use tools and form lasting social bonds — who was she?
Committed to accuracy and verification, this occupation and set of methods involves gathering and distributing the day's news — what field is it?
Journalism: Production of reports on current events.
Named from a Wiradjuri word imitating its own call, this Australian tree kingfisher's cackling laugh is a go-to sound effect for movie jungle scenes — what is it?
Kookaburra: Genus of birds (terrestrial tree kingfishers)
Together with pikas, this mammal family — comprising rabbits and hares — makes up the order Lagomorpha and includes over 70 species — which family?
Leporidae: Family of lagomorphs. Leporidae is the family of rabbits and hares (Lepus), containing over 70 species of extant mammals in all.
Developed under Kelly Johnson's Skunk Works team after the discovery of Germany's Me 262, this aircraft became the first jet fighter flown operationally by U.S. forces in World War II — which jet?
Lockheed P-80 Shooting Star: First jet aircraft in U.S. operational service.
Best known in its heptahydrate form as Epsom salt, this white crystalline compound (MgSO4) is also used in agriculture to fix soils deficient in an essential plant nutrient — what compound is it?
Magnesium sulfate: Chemical compound with formula MgSO4.
Awarded the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering energy quanta, this German physicist originated quantum theory and lent his name to a fundamental physical constant — who is he?
Sold under the brand name Robaxin and developed in 1956, this centrally acting muscle relaxant treats short-term musculoskeletal pain but its exact mechanism remains unclear — what is it?
Methocarbamol: Medication for musculoskeletal pain. It may be used together with rest, physical therapy, and pain medication.
Following the S phase and ending in cytokinesis, this equational cell division splits replicated chromosomes into two genetically identical daughter nuclei — what is the process called?
Mitosis: Cell division into two identical cells. Mitosis is a part of the cell cycle in eukaryotic cells in which replicated chromosomes are separated into two new nuclei.
Taking its name from the Latin for 'weasel,' this is the largest family in the suborder Caniformia — gathering otters, badgers, martens, and wolverines under one roof. What is it?
Described by Eric Kandel as the 'epic challenge' of biology, this multidisciplinary field studies the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system — what field is it?
Neuroscience: Scientific study of the nervous system.
Named for a discredited belief that it 'rows' itself with its pelvic fins, this family of long pelagic fish includes the longest bony fish alive at up to 8 meters?
Oarfish: Pelagic lampriform fish belonging to Regalecidae.
Working alongside Lise Meitner and Fritz Strassmann in 1938, this German chemist co-discovered nuclear fission and later won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone — who is he?
Otto Hahn: German nuclear chemist and Nobel laureate (1879–1968)

He joined the British Astronomical Association at age 11, compiled the Caldwell catalogue, and hosted the BBC's "The Sky at Night" — the longest-running TV series with its original presenter. Who was this English amateur astronomer?
Patrick Moore: English astronomer, broadcaster and writer (1923–2012)
Found naturally in chocolate — especially after fermentation — this trace amine stimulates the central nervous system by binding to a receptor called TAAR1. What compound is it?
Phenethylamine: Organic compound, a stimulant in humans.

Often at its worst with the very first steps of the day, this common foot disorder inflames the connective tissue supporting the arch and is linked to tight calf muscles and heel spurs — what condition is it?

Plantar fasciitis: Connective tissue disorder of the heel. Plantar fasciitis or plantar heel pain is a disorder of the plantar fascia, which is the connective tissue that supports the arch of the foot.
Sold under the brand name Lyrica, this anticonvulsant amino-acid drug also treats fibromyalgia, nerve pain, and anxiety — which medication is it?
Pregabalin: Anticonvulsant medication. Its use in epilepsy is as an add-on therapy for partial seizures.
This water-soluble organic compound, made of two fused rings, gives its name to a class that includes DNA's adenine and guanine bases — what is it?
Named for the way light stretches toward longer wavelengths, this phenomenon comes in Doppler, gravitational, and cosmological forms and is measured by the value z — what is it?
Redshift: Change in wavelength of light.
This British economist, who won the 1991 Nobel and spent decades at the University of Chicago Law School, urged the field to study real-world wealth creation in Adam Smith's spirit — who was he?
Ronald Coase: British economist and Nobel laureate (1910–2013)
First known as a portrait painter, this American inventor helped develop a single-wire telegraph system and lent his name to the dot-and-dash code introduced in 1837 — who is he?
Samuel Morse: American inventor and painter (1791–1872)
This secretive Soviet chief designer built the rocket that launched the first satellite, the first animal in orbit, and the first human into space — who was he?

Thanks to extra joints in its skull, this legless, scale-covered reptile can swallow prey far bigger than its own head — and its paired organs sit one behind the other to fit a narrow body. What creature is it?
Working largely in isolation, this early-20th-century Indian mathematician solved problems thought unsolvable, though leading professionals first dismissed his work as too novel — who was he?

Encompassing everything from the electrical telegraph to modern radio, this field is defined as the transmission of information over distance using electrical or electronic means — what field is it?
Telecommunications: Transmission of information electromagnetically. The physical limitations of metallic media prompted the development of optical fibre.
This blood-feeding arachnid's oldest fossils date back roughly 100 million years to the Cretaceous, and it comes in two main flavors: hard-bodied and soft-bodied — which parasite?
Tick: Order of arachnids in the arthropod phylum.
Named for its three-lobed shape, this extinct marine arthropod left over 22,000 fossilized species behind after roughly 270 million years in ancient oceans. What creature is it?
Trilobite: Class of extinct, Paleozoic arthropods.
Before becoming the first woman in space aboard a solo 1963 flight that orbited Earth 48 times, this cosmonaut worked in a textile factory and skydove as a hobby — who is she?
Valentina Tereshkova: Russian cosmonaut and politician (born 1937)
Equal to one joule per second, this SI unit of power honors an 18th-century Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine in 1776 — which unit is it?
Watt: SI derived unit of power. The watt (symbol: W) is the unit of power or radiant flux in the International System of Units (SI), equal to 1 joule per second or 1 kg⋅m2⋅s−3.
Native to South America and first cultivated by the Guaraní people, the steeped leaves of this holly-genus plant produce a caffeinated beverage — what is it?
Yerba mate: South American holly plant. Yerba mate or yerba maté ( YUR-bə MAH-tay), Ilex paraguariensis, is a plant species of the holly genus native to South America.

The symbol for platinum is Pt. Platinum is a chemical element; it has symbol Pt and atomic number 78.
